rows.experiment_summary: This first experiment established a baseline using an RNA-only, single-profile model with PCA (2000 components) and no image modality, aggregation, or fusion. The validation accuracy of ~48.5% (F1 ~46.4%) is an initial observation indicating that the raw PCA-reduced RNA signal alone yields modest predictive performance, though it is unclear whether this reflects the ceiling for RNA-only approaches or simply the floor before added complexity. It remains uncertain whether learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, or cross-modal fusion could substantially improve beyond this baseline, and whether the task is broadly solvable at higher accuracy levels.
rows.selection_reason: 1) No prior evidence exists, so the critical uncertainty is whether the task is solvable at all and what the performance floor looks like. 2) config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest viable configuration: a single RNA profile reduced by PCA with no aggregation or fusion. It establishes a clean baseline that isolates the raw predictive signal in the RNA data without confounding from encoder choice, profile multiplicity, or cross-modal fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, starting with the cheapest, most interpretable experiment is the most efficient first step: it is fast to train, provides a reference point against which every added complexity (better encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, fusion strategy) can be measured, and avoids prematurely investing in complex multimodal or learned-encoder configurations whose marginal value over a simple PCA baseline is still unknown.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment established an image-only, single-profile baseline using a ResNet50 encoder with no aggregation or fusion, yielding a validation accuracy of ~20.8% (F1 ~17.2%), which is substantially lower than the RNA-only PCA baseline of ~48.5%. This initial observation suggests that, under this configuration, the image modality carries considerably weaker independent predictive signal than the RNA modality, though the comparison is confounded by differing encoder choices (learned ResNet50 vs. linear PCA) and cannot definitively isolate modality as the sole cause of the gap. It remains uncertain whether alternative image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or a different architectural setup could substantially improve the image signal, and whether even a weak image contribution might still add value in a multimodal fusion setting.
rows.selection_reason: With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → ~48.5% acc), we have zero evidence about whether the image modality carries any independent predictive signal. This is the single most important uncertainty to resolve before investing in any multimodal or fusion configurations. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the simplest, cleanest image-only baseline: it changes exactly one high-level dimension (modality) relative to config_001 while keeping profile setting, aggregation, and fusion at their minimal defaults. If image alone approaches or exceeds the RNA baseline, it confirms the image modality is informative and justifies pursuing multimodal fusion (configs 016–051). If image alone is substantially worse, it tells us to focus the remaining budget on improving the RNA side (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation) rather than spending experiments on multimodal configurations that may not benefit from a weak second modality. This experiment maximizes information gain per trial under a limited budget by resolving a binary, strategy-shaping question that no other single experiment can answer.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the effect of representation quality by replacing the linear PCA-2000 encoder with a learned scvi_n200 variational autoencoder in the otherwise identical RNA-only, single-profile configuration. The validation accuracy improved from ~48.5% (F1 ~46.4%) to ~52.0% (F1 ~49.8%), a modest ~3.5-point gain that indicates a learned nonlinear encoder captures some additional structure beyond linear PCA, yet the relatively small improvement also suggests the single-profile RNA signal may be partially data-limited rather than purely representation-limited. It remains uncertain whether this encoder advantage would compound in multiprofile aggregation or multimodal fusion settings, and whether the ~52% level is near the practical ceiling for RNA-only single-profile models or whether further architectural changes could yield substantially larger gains.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA-2000) achieved 48.5% acc, while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50) achieved only 20.8% acc. The RNA modality is clearly the stronger signal, but we have no evidence yet on whether the PCA representation is near its ceiling or whether a learned nonlinear encoder could substantially improve it. Question: config_004 (RNA-only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a single-variable change from config_001—only the RNA encoder shifts from linear PCA to a learned variational autoencoder—so it cleanly isolates the effect of representation quality. Why this is the best next step: (1) It directly tests whether the 48.5% baseline is a representation limitation or a data limitation, which fundamentally shapes all downstream decisions (multiprofile, fusion, encoder choice). (2) If scvi substantially outperforms PCA, we gain a strong prior for using learned encoders in multiprofile and multimodal settings, making later experiments more targeted. If it does not, we learn that the RNA signal is inherently limited under these conditions and can redirect budget toward aggregation or fusion. (3) It avoids the confound of simultaneously changing encoder, profile setting, and aggregation, keeping the comparison interpretable under a tight budget.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested the effect of multiprofile aggregation via avgpool on the RNA-only, scvi_n200 configuration, directly comparable to the single-profile scvi_n200 baseline (llm_summary_003). The validation accuracy rose from ~52.0% to ~65.0% (F1 from ~49.8% to ~62.8%), a substantial ~13-point gain indicating that aggregating multiple profiles adds significant signal beyond a single profile and is a high-leverage axis of improvement, far exceeding the ~3.5-point encoder-quality gain observed earlier. It remains uncertain whether more complex aggregation strategies (e.g., transformer) could push beyond ~65%, whether this gain compounds with cross-modal fusion or alternative encoders, and whether the previously weak image modality might contribute more in a multiprofile context.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: Three experiments establish that RNA is the dominant modality (~48-52% vs ~21% for image) and that the learned scvi_n200 encoder outperforms PCA-2000 by ~3.5 points in the single-profile setting. However, all experiments so far are single-profile; the effect of multiprofile aggregation is completely untested. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) adds meaningful signal beyond a single profile, and whether the encoder advantage of scvi_n200 compounds or diminishes under aggregation. This experiment (config_005: rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) tests the single design decision of adding multiprofile + avgpool on top of the best-known RNA encoder, directly comparable to config_004. If it yields a substantial gain over 52%, aggregation is a key axis to exploit; if the gain is marginal, it tells us the single-profile RNA signal is near its ceiling and we should pivot to testing fusion or alternative encoders. This is the highest-information next step because it resolves the most critical unexplored axis (profile/aggregation) while keeping the encoder at its best-validated setting, and it uses the simpler avgpool before committing to the more complex transformer.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the aggregation architecture by replacing avgpool with a transformer in the otherwise identical RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200 configuration (directly comparable to llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy of ~65.3% (F1 ~62.8%) is essentially unchanged from the avgpool result of ~65.0% (F1 ~62.8%), a negligible ~0.3-point difference suggesting that transformer aggregation does not substantially outperform simple average pooling and that ~65% may represent a practical ceiling for RNA-only multiprofile models under this encoder. It remains uncertain whether alternative encoders, the previously weak image modality in a multiprofile context, or cross-modal fusion could push beyond this level, and whether the near-equivalence of aggregation strategies would hold under different data scales or architectural combinations.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: Multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) produced the largest single gain observed (~13 points, 52%→65%), making aggregation the highest-leverage design axis. The scvi_n200 encoder added a modest +3.5 points over PCA, and image-only signal is very weak (~21%). Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the aggregation *strategy* (avgpool vs. transformer) matters, or whether ~65% is near the RNA-only ceiling. This experiment (config_006) directly tests transformer aggregation in an otherwise identical setup to config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200), isolating the aggregation architecture as the sole variable. If transformer substantially improves over avgpool, it signals that richer aggregation will be critical in multimodal fusion and justifies prioritizing transformer-based configs later. If it does not, it confirms avgpool is near-optimal, simplifying the search space and letting us focus budget on encoder choice or fusion strategy. This is the best use of the next experiment because it exploits the strongest evidence (multiprofile is the key lever) while reducing uncertainty on a sub-decision that will gate many future multimodal configurations, all without introducing the additional confounds of a new modality or encoder.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested whether multiprofile avgpool aggregation could recover meaningful signal from the image modality, directly paralleling the RNA multiprofile experiment (llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy of ~32.8% (F1 ~28.8%) represents a ~12-point improvement over the image-only single-profile baseline (~20.8%, llm_summary_002), confirming that the single-profile limitation was a contributing factor to the image modality's apparent weakness, yet the image modality remains substantially weaker than the RNA-only multiprofile baseline (~65.0%). This suggests the image modality carries considerably less independent predictive signal than RNA even after multiprofile aggregation, though it remains uncertain whether alternative image encoders, more complex aggregation, or multimodal fusion could extract additional value from the residual image signal, and whether ~32.8% is near the practical ceiling for image-only multiprofile models.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: The image-only single-profile baseline (config_010) yielded only ~20.8% accuracy, far below the RNA-only baselines, but this was tested with a single profile. For RNA, moving from single-profile to multi-profile was the single largest lever discovered (+13 points, config_004→config_005). It is currently unknown whether the image modality's apparent weakness is due to an inherent lack of signal or simply the single-profile limitation. Question tested: config_011 (image-only, multi-profile, ResNet50, avgpool) directly parallels the RNA multi-profile experiment and isolates whether multi-profile aggregation recovers meaningful image signal. Why this is the best next experiment: The result will determine whether any multimodal fusion experiment is worth pursuing. If image multi-profile remains very weak (~20-30%), it strongly suggests the image modality carries little independent signal and budget should be redirected to RNA-only improvements (e.g., scgpt encoder). If it jumps substantially, it validates the image modality and justifies investing in multimodal fusion configs. This single, clean experiment resolves a major branch of the search tree and avoids committing budget to multimodal configurations whose value is currently unestablished.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested whether adding the image modality (ResNet50, avgpool) via simple concat fusion to the strongest RNA-only multiprofile backbone (scvi_n200, avgpool) would push beyond the ~65% RNA-only ceiling. The validation accuracy of ~63.2% (F1 ~60.7%) is slightly below the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool baseline (~65.0%), an initial observation suggesting that the residual image signal does not provide complementary predictive information under this configuration and may introduce mild interference, though the ~1.8-point gap is small and the specific contributor (image content, ResNet50 encoder quality, or the concat mechanism) cannot be isolated from this single experiment. It remains uncertain whether alternative fusion strategies (e.g., weighted or attention-based), stronger image encoders, or different image-branch aggregation could recover or exceed the RNA-only performance, or whether the image modality is fundamentally non-complementary for this task.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: The best result so far is ~65.3% (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer; config_006), with avgpool essentially equivalent at ~65.0% (config_005). The image modality alone is weak (~32.8% multiprofile, config_011), but it remains entirely untested whether image adds complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation. This is the largest remaining design uncertainty. Question: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly extends the best RNA-only multiprofile setup by adding the image modality via simple concat fusion, using the same resnet50 encoder for which we already have a single-modality baseline. It isolates the fusion question: does the residual image signal contribute beyond the ~65% RNA-only ceiling? Why this is the best next experiment: it tests the highest-leverage unexplored axis (cross-modal fusion) with the strongest known RNA backbone and the simplest reasonable fusion/aggregation choices, avoiding confounds. If it exceeds 65%, we confirm multimodal fusion is productive and can then optimize fusion strategy (weighted) and image encoder (ViT-L). If it does not, we learn the image modality is not complementary under this setup and can redirect budget toward RNA-only encoder improvements (e.g., scgpt) or alternative image encoders. No other single experiment reduces as much uncertainty about the most impactful remaining design decision.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the fusion mechanism by replacing concat with weighted fusion in the otherwise identical multimodal, multiprofile configuration (scvi_n200 + ResNet50, avgpool), directly comparable to llm_summary_007. Validation accuracy rose from ~63.2% to ~67.8% (F1 from ~60.7% to ~64.6%), a ~4.6-point gain attributable to the fusion change, and now exceeds the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool baseline (~65.0%, llm_summary_004) by ~2.8 points, indicating that the image modality does carry complementary signal that concat fails to exploit and that weighted fusion effectively down-weights the weaker image contribution. It remains uncertain whether attention-based or learned fusion could push further beyond ~67.8%, whether stronger image encoders or image-specific aggregation could amplify the residual image contribution, and whether this gain is stable across different data splits or task formulations.
rows.selection_reason: The strongest RNA-only multiprofile baseline (scvi_n200, avgpool) achieves ~65.0% accuracy, but adding the image modality via concat fusion (config_030) actually *decreased* performance to ~63.2%. The critical uncertainty is whether this ~1.8-point drop is caused by the concat fusion mechanism (which treats both modalities equally and cannot down-weight a weak signal) or by the image content itself being non-complementary. Config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, keeping all other settings identical to config_030 (scvi_n200, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool). This single-variable comparison isolates the fusion strategy: if weighted fusion recovers to ≥65%, it indicates the image carries complementary signal that concat fails to exploit; if it remains below 65%, it strongly suggests the ResNet50-encoded image is fundamentally non-complementary under this setup, saving budget from further image-encoder or aggregation variants. This is the most information-dense next experiment because it directly addresses the key open question (can multimodal beat RNA-only?) with minimal confounding, and the answer will determine whether subsequent budget should go toward stronger image encoders or toward RNA-only encoder exploration (e.g., scgpt).

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the effect of image encoder quality by replacing ResNet50 with ImageNet ViT-L in the otherwise identical multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted-fusion configuration (directly comparable to llm_summary_008). Validation accuracy rose from ~67.8% to ~70.6% (F1 from ~64.6% to ~66.7%), a ~2.8-point gain attributable to the encoder swap, indicating that the image branch was at least partially encoder-limited and that a stronger visual representation can amplify the complementary signal exploited by weighted fusion. It remains uncertain whether further encoder improvements, alternative image-branch aggregation, or different fusion mechanisms could push beyond ~70.6%, and whether the residual image contribution is now approaching a data-limited ceiling.
rows.selection_reason: The current best configuration (config_031, 67.8% acc) uses weighted fusion to successfully leverage a weak image signal (~2.8 points above RNA-only multiprofile). The image modality remains the weakest component (image-only multiprofile: 32.8% vs RNA-only multiprofile: 65.0%), and we have only tested ResNet50 as the image encoder. Config_037 replaces ResNet50 with ImageNet ViT-L in the otherwise identical multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted-fusion setup, isolating the effect of image encoder quality. If ViT-L substantially improves the image branch, the weighted fusion should amplify the complementary signal and push beyond 67.8%; if not, it confirms the image modality is fundamentally data-limited rather than encoder-limited. This is a single-variable change from the current best, making it the most informative and efficient next step: it directly exploits the strongest evidence (weighted fusion works, multiprofile is critical) while reducing uncertainty about whether the residual image contribution can be amplified with a stronger representation.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the RNA encoder by substituting scgpt for scvi_n200 in the otherwise identical RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool configuration (directly comparable to llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy of ~53.0% (F1 ~51.5%) is approximately 12 points below the scvi_n200 result (~65.0%, F1 ~62.8%), a substantial gap cleanly attributable to the encoder swap, indicating that scgpt captures considerably less predictive structure than scvi_n200 for this task. This result suggests the scgpt branch of the search space is unlikely to be competitive and can be deprioritized, though it remains uncertain whether scgpt might behave differently under multimodal fusion, alternative aggregation strategies, or different data scales.
rows.selection_reason: The current best (config_037, 70.6%) uses scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder, but scgpt has not been tested in any configuration. Since RNA is the dominant signal source (RNA-only multiprofile achieves ~65% vs. image-only ~33%), the RNA encoder choice is a high-leverage axis. Config_008 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) directly parallels config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, 65.0%), changing only the RNA encoder. This cleanly isolates whether scgpt captures more predictive structure than scvi_n200. If scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, the gain could compound with multiprofile aggregation, weighted fusion, and ViT-L in a follow-up multimodal experiment. If it does not, an entire branch of the search space (all scgpt configurations) is effectively ruled out, saving future budget for other axes. This is preferred over testing scgpt directly in the full multimodal setting (e.g., config_049) because the simpler RNA-only comparison provides cleaner attribution, and over testing transformer aggregation in the multimodal setting (config_039) because transformer≈avgpool is already well-established from the RNA-only evidence.
